Here in the Swedish countryside, right here in Djärkster, lies a sacred site that has witnessed over 3,000 years of rituals and offerings. But what were these mysterious carvings really for? Let's take a closer look. Petroglyphs like these found all across Scandinavia are more than just art, and you depict warriors, ships, animals, and symbols of the sun. But among them you'll often find small, round depressions, and these are some of the most intriguing of all. Archaeologists believe these were use in fertility rituals, both for the land and for people. Some were filled with butter, milk, or grain, offerings meant to nourish the earth and promise a good harvest. Others may have held blood, returning life energy to the land in return for prosperity. Women struggling to conceive would rub their stomachs, or lower regions. Over these marks, believing the spirits within the stone could bless them with children. Some even drank the water that pulled inside, convinced it carried sacred power, and remarkably some of these customs lasted well into the medieval era. Many school group that are found near solar symbols. Suggesting they were linked to the life-giving power of the sun, the sun was everything, its return in spring meant survival, and its absence in winter brought hardship. Perhaps these rituals were a way of binding themselves to the forces that govern their world, bleeding for life, light, and abundance. Even today some farmers still pour milk or beer on these stones for good luck, and this is just one of many such sites scattered across Scandinavia. There's a man in the forests of Sweden holding up a ship and he's been doing it for 3,000 years. This is the Branskog Sweatbeth, one of the largest and most detailed Bronze Age petroglyphs in all of Scandinavia. Over four meters long it shows six men rowing a boat. At both ends of the ship are animal heads, probably moose, which held spiritual significance in the Nordic Bronze Age. The most mysterious part is that beneath the stern there is a life-sized human figure, looking as if he's holding the ship above him. Some believe that it's the giant Eregyr, the king of the sea giants, known for hosting the gods in his underwater hall. It could also represent the dead being carried into the afterlife. Back in the Branses, this wasn't a forest. This stone sat right beside the sea and was used as a ritual site. Today it's far inland thanks to post-glacial at Landerise. Nobody knows the whole story, but somebody 3,000 years ago thought it was worthy enough to preserve.

Recorded on thousands of maps but never actually found, this is Heebrasil. Heebrasil is shrouded in fog and visible for just one day every seven years. Even then, reaching it was said to be impossible. Hee is an old Gaelic word for island, and Brasil comes from descendants or clan of Brícal, who was an ancient figure linked from nobility and greatness in early Irish law. The first recorded appearance of Heebrasil was on nautical charts in 1325, and for centuries afterwards maps from around the world placed around the island in the Atlantic, complete with a river bisecting it. Sailors and villagers claimed sightings throughout the ages. Some described green meadows and woodlands before it faded back into the mist. This tried to explore it but only found sea where it once seemed to stand. Said to be a place where nobody aged and there was eternal peace. An Irish physician from the Olí family claimed he was transported this island and gifted a manuscript of cures. A real 15th century medical codex which is now stored at the Royal Irish Academy. Despite centuries of fascination, Heebrasil slipped from the charts by the late 1800s, with its final appearances noted around 1873. By this point it appeared on thousands of maps for over 600 years. The Norse gods were never one tribe. One came with thunder and the other came with harvest. Their war shaped the Europe that we know today. There were two tribes, the Æsir and the Vánir. Their war may be the oldest memory of our ancestors, when two different peoples of Europe first met. The Æsir were sky gods. Odin, Thor, Tyr, they ruled through strength, storms and order. They can be traced back to the Indo-European warrior culture that swept into Europe thousands of years ago. The same culture that gave rise to the thunder gods of India, the Baltics and the Gaelic tribes. But the farmers of Europe had their own gods. The Vánir, Frey, Freyja, Njord, were gods of the land, fertility and the sea. They belonged to the old farming world of Europe, where life followed the land and seasons. Their temples were built on fertile ground and their rituals were tied to harvest. When these two cultures met, their gods went to war. The war of the Æsir and the Vánir. Yet neither side could win, so they made peace. Exchanging hostages and sharing their wisdom. From that peace was born the belief system that we know today. Odin and Frey, sky and soil and warrior and farmer. All part of one divine family. The Norse gods tell an ancient story. Northern Europe itself was forged from two peoples, one of the heavens and one of the earth. Their war ended in unity. Every storm that feeds the soil, every harvest after thunder, still remembers them both.

Have you ever heard this enchanting and completely unique Swedish instrument? The nikkelharpa, which translates to keyed harp, has roots stretching back to over 650 years ago in Sweden. The oldest depiction of the nikkelharpa is from 1350 in Schellangasjkotland and has since become a staple in Swedish folk music and also Sweden's national instrument. What makes the nikkelharpa so special is its intricate mechanics. It is a bowed instrument, but what sets it apart are the wooden keys along its neck. These keys press against the strings, creating different notes, and the resonant ethereal sound comes from its sympathetic strings, which are not played on, but instead vibrate along, making just one nikkelharpa sound like a whole orchestra. Beneath this ancient mound in Wales lies a neolithic time capsule. Bryn Kelly Dee, meaning the Mound in the Dark Grove, is one of Wales' most intriguing prehistoric monuments. Let's take a look inside. This six metre passage leads to a central chamber, where a single pillar still stands after 50 centuries. Constructed around 5000 years ago, it first served as a henge, a circular earthwork with a ring of standing stones, before being repurposed as a burial site. Archaeologists discovered cremated human remains here, suggesting that it was a place of burial, but its role is more than just a tomb. The entrance passage is aligned with the rising sun and the summer solstice, meaning that once a year sunlight floods into the interior chamber. This alignment signifies a deep ritual significance, perhaps a ceremony marking the turning of the year, or a belief in afterlife connected to the sun cycle. Standing stones nearby may have played a role in these rituals, possibly used for offerings or ancestor worship. The carved patternstone here decorated with swirling design might represent spiritual or astronomical meanings, but its exact purpose remains unknown. Ryn Kelly Dee is a glimpse into the belief systems of our Neolithic thought-beth, where life, death and the cosmos were intertwined. Today visitors still leave small offerings inside, flowers, coins and stones as a mark of respect to their ancestors.

Did our pagan ancestors really throw elderly off of cliffs? Or is this just another lie to paint our pagan ancestors as barbaric? You may have heard of the so-called Eta Stupa, a ritual where the elderly in law society were forced to jump to their deaths when they became old and a burden. Sounds brutal, doesn't it? Well, it never actually happened. The earliest mentions of Eta Stupa don't come from the Viking Age. They come from 17th and 18th century Christian scholars, long after paganism had been overthrown. There is no mention of the Eta Stupa in any ancient law codes, any Eddas or the Sargas. Swedish historian Nils Arnlund debunked this in the early 1900s, pointing out that the so-called Eta Super sites were actually just steep cliffs with no evidence of ritual use. So where did this idea come from? It was likely a way to demonize pre-Christian Europe, just like the bloodthirsty Vikings and child-sacrificing Druids the Chomes. It served to justify the destruction of indigenous European beliefs. The truth is that elders in pagan societies were deeply respected. They were the storytellers, the lawkeepers, the ones that passed down the wisdom. In Norse culture, old warriors might seek a final battle for them. But being thrown off a cliff, that should propaganda. So next time someone tells you that our ancestors were savages, remind them history is written by the victors.

Were you aware that the name England comes from a Norse god? Let me explain. Our story begins with the Angles, a Germanic tribe from the Anglal Peninsula. Their name gave rise to Englaland, the land of the Angles, which evolved into England. In the fifth century, the Angles, alongside the Saxons and the Jutes, migrated into Britain. Here's the interesting part. The Angles were part of the Ingveones, a group of tribes who revered the deity Ingvi Freyr, or simply Freyr. A Norse god associated with male fertility and prosperity. Freyr is also the patron god of Sweden. So the name England is the legacy of the Angles and their divine patron Freyr.

In the mountains of Snowdonia lies Hlyn Idwal, a lake named after a young prince whose tragic story has been passed down for centuries. Idwal was the son of Owain Gwyneth, a 12th century king. Unlike his father who was a warrior, Idwal was known for his peaceful nature. So he was sent away from the dangers of war to be cared for by his uncle Nevith. But Nevith was not trustworthy. According to legend, he saw Idwal as a threat to his own power. The story goes that he arranged for Idwal to die here at the lake. Some say that he was drowned, but others say that he was killed here and his body left in the water. What is certain is that his father never forgave his betrayal and said that this lake should always bear his son's name. Over time, Hlyn Idwal became linked with superstition. Local shepherds believed that no birds would fly over it, seeing it as a sign that the lake was cast. The nearby cliffs known as Tuthi, or Devil's Kitchen, have a reputation for mystery. Mist often rises from the dark clefs in the rock, leading to stories of druids using the site for rituals. But beyond its legends, Hlyn Idwal is also an important natural site. It is home to rare alpine plants that have survived here since the last ifage. One of these is the Snowdon Lily, which only grows in a few places in Snowdonia.
